title: Excretory System

toc.title: 8.1 Excretory organs and the structure of the nephron
8.2 Formation of urine and its regulation

html:
The excretory system carries 2 of the 40 Zoology questions.

The paper builds them from three blocks: the organs and the nephron (what each part is and does), the formation of urine (filtration, reabsorption, secretion, the counter-current multiplier and the three hormones that set urine volume), and the disorders (nephritis, stones, failure, dialysis).

Almost every question turns on a direction, a number or a permeability: which limb lets water through, which hormone makes urine small, which value is the renal threshold.

The three traps that decide marks are the descending limb is permeable to water and the ascending limb is not, ADH increases water reabsorption so its deficiency gives a large dilute urine, and the posterior pituitary stores ADH but the hypothalamus makes it.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Organs: a pair of kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder and the urethra, plus the accessory routes — skin (sweat), lungs (CO₂ and water vapour) and liver (urea from deamination, bile pigments).
  • Kidney in section: capsule → cortex (glomeruli, convoluted tubules) → medulla (pyramids, loops, collecting ducts) → renal pelvis → ureter; about 1 million nephrons per kidney.
  • Nephron: Bowman's capsule with podocytes, PCT with a brush border, the loop of Henle, DCT with the macula densa, the collecting duct, and the peritubular capillaries/vasa recta.
  • Ultrafiltration: pores and negative charge hold back cells and plasma proteins; net filtration pressure ≈ 10 mmHg; GFR ≈ 125 mL min⁻¹ = 180 L day⁻¹.
  • Reabsorption: 100 % of glucose and amino acids by active transport in the PCT; water by osmosis; the counter-current multiplier builds a gradient of 300 → 1200 mOsm L⁻¹.
  • Secretion: H⁺, K⁺, NH₃ and drugs; the tubule's route for acid–base control.
  • Hormones: ADH (water, collecting duct), aldosterone (Na⁺ in, K⁺ out), ANP (Na⁺ and water out); each changes both the volume and the concentration of urine.
  • Disorders: nephritis, calculi, acute and chronic failure, haemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis, transplantation.

8.1 Excretory organs and the structure of the nephron

Excretion, egestion and secretion

Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism from the body — substances that were made inside cells and can no longer be used.

It is not the same as egestion, which is the removal of unabsorbed food from the gut, nor as secretion, which is the release of a useful substance such as a hormone or an enzyme.

The nitrogenous waste depends on the animal's habitat. Ammonotelic animals (bony fish, aquatic invertebrates, tadpoles) excrete ammonia, which is very toxic but dissolves easily in plentiful water.

Ureotelic animals (man, mammals, adult frogs, cartilaginous fish) spend energy converting ammonia to urea, which is far less toxic and can be carried in a small volume of water.

Uricotelic animals (birds, reptiles, insects) convert it to uric acid, which is almost insoluble and is passed as a paste — the best saving of water, at the greatest energy cost.

The organs

Organ Structure What it removes
Kidney (a pair) bean-shaped, retroperitoneal, T12–L3 urea, uric acid, creatinine, excess salts, water, H⁺; also makes renin and erythropoietin
Ureter (a pair) muscular tube, 25–30 cm, peristaltic carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder
Urinary bladder muscular sac with transitional epithelium and the detrusor muscle stores urine (300–400 mL, up to 600–800 mL)
Urethra female ≈ 4 cm, male ≈ 20 cm carries urine out; in the male it also carries semen

Accessory excretory organs

  • Skin — sweat glands remove water, sodium chloride, urea and lactic acid; sebaceous glands remove sebum. Sweat is not a major route for nitrogen in man, but it matters in fever and heavy work.
  • Lungs — remove carbon dioxide and water vapour at every breath.
  • Liver — deaminates surplus amino acids and hands the ammonia to the urea cycle (ornithine cycle), so urea is made here; it also breaks down haemoglobin and excretes bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin) into bile, and detoxifies drugs and alcohol.
  • Large intestine — carries bile pigments and cholesterol out in faeces.
Excretion is not only urine

A question that asks "which organ removes nitrogenous waste" may offer the liver as well as the kidney. The liver makes urea; the kidney excretes it. Both are correct answers to different stems, so read which verb is used.

The spleen is not an excretory organ — it destroys old red cells, but the pigment it produces is passed to the liver.

Position, coverings and blood supply

Each kidney is about 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide and 3 cm thick, and weighs 130–150 g. It lies behind the peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left because the liver pushes it down.

The medial border has a notch, the hilum, through which the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave. The hilum opens into a cavity, the renal sinus, filled with fat and the pelvis.

Three coverings protect it: the inner fibrous capsule, a middle perirenal fat cushion and the outer renal fascia.

The blood supply is a trap in itself:

Renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries or vasa recta → interlobular vein → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein.

The kidney receives about 1.2 L of blood per minute, roughly a quarter of the cardiac output.

The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent, so blood damps up in the glomerulus and the pressure there stays high — that is what drives filtration.

The second capillary bed (peritubular and vasa recta) is at low pressure, which is what allows reabsorption.

The kidney in section

Region Contents Job
Cortex renal corpuscles (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule), PCT and DCT, peritubular capillaries filtration and most reabsorption
Medulla 8–18 renal pyramids, loops of Henle, collecting ducts, vasa recta builds the osmotic gradient; concentrates urine
Renal columns (of Bertin) cortical tissue between the pyramids carry interlobar vessels
Papilla the apex of each pyramid drips urine into a minor calyx
Renal pelvis funnel formed by major calyces collects urine and passes it to the ureter

The nephron

A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney; each kidney holds about one million. There are two kinds. Cortical nephrons (about 85 %) sit high in the cortex with short loops that barely enter the medulla.

Juxtamedullary nephrons (about 15 %) lie near the medulla and have long loops running deep into it; only they can build the steep gradient needed for concentrated urine.

Segment Epithelium Main job
Bowman's capsule outer parietal layer of squamous cells; inner visceral layer of podocytes receives the filtrate
Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) cuboidal with a brush border of microvilli and many mitochondria 65–70 % of reabsorption: all glucose and amino acids, most Na⁺, water and HCO₃⁻
Descending limb thin squamous water leaves by osmosis; solutes stay
Ascending limb thin then thick cuboidal impermeable to water; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ pumped out (the "diluting segment")
Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) cuboidal, no brush border Na⁺ reabsorption under aldosterone, Ca²⁺ under PTH, K⁺ and H⁺ secretion
Collecting duct principal cells and intercalated cells water under ADH; final acid–base adjustment; urea recycling
Peritubular capillaries / vasa recta endothelium take back water and solutes; the vasa recta is a counter-current exchanger

The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) sits where the DCT touches its own afferent arteriole.

It has three parts: the macula densa (tall, crowded cells of the DCT that sense Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the filtrate), the juxtaglomerular cells (smooth-muscle-like cells of the afferent arteriole that store renin) and the extraglomerular mesangial cells between them.

This is the sensor that starts the renin–angiotensin system when blood pressure or sodium falls.

8.2 Formation of urine and its regulation

Urine is made in three processes, in this order: ultrafiltration in the renal corpuscle, selective reabsorption along the tubule, and tubular secretion from the blood into the tubule. A fourth process, concentration, happens in the collecting duct under ADH.

Step 1 — ultrafiltration

Blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule. The barrier has three layers:

Layer Structure What it holds back
Fenestrated endothelium pores 70–100 nm blood cells
Basement membrane glycoproteins and collagen, negatively charged large proteins; the charge repels albumin
Podocyte slit diaphragms foot processes with slits about 4–7 nm medium proteins

So the filtrate is almost protein-free: water, glucose, amino acids, urea, uric acid, creatinine, ions and small peptides pass; cells and plasma proteins do not.

Albumin (69 kDa) is held back by both its size and its negative charge — a question that offers only "size" is incomplete when "size and charge" is available.

The pressures at the glomerulus are:

P_{\text{net}} = P_{\text{glomerular}} - (P_{\text{oncotic}} + P_{\text{capsular}}) = 55 - (30 + 15) = 10\ \text{mmHg}

Pressure Value
Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure 55 mmHg (high because the efferent arteriole is narrow)
Plasma oncotic pressure (proteins pull water back) 30 mmHg
Capsular hydrostatic pressure 15 mmHg
Net filtration pressure 10 mmHg

GFR (glomerular filtration rate) is about 125 mL min⁻¹, i.e. 180 L day⁻¹ — the whole plasma volume filtered about 60 times a day. The filtration fraction is GFR ÷ renal plasma flow = 125 ÷ 625 = 20 %.

How much filtrate is reabsorbed

Problem. A student has a GFR of 125 mL min⁻¹ and passes 1.5 L of urine a day. What volume is reabsorbed, and what percentage is that?

Solution. Filtrate per day = 125 \times 60 \times 24 = 180\,000 mL = 180 L. Reabsorbed = 180 - 1.5 = 178.5 L. Percentage = 178.5/180 \times 100 = 99.2\ \%. So about 99 % of the filtrate is taken back; only 1 % leaves as urine.

What is filtered is not what is excreted

The filtrate contains glucose, but normal urine does not, because the PCT reabsorbs it. A stem that says "glucose is not filtered" is wrong; glucose is filtered and then completely reabsorbed. The same is true of amino acids and most bicarbonate.

Estimating GFR from creatinine clearance

Problem. A patient collects 1.5 L of urine in 24 hours. Urine creatinine is 100 mg/dL and plasma creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. What is the creatinine clearance, and is it normal?

Solution. Amount excreted per day = 100\ \text{mg/dL} \times 15\ \text{dL} = 1500 mg. Clearance = excretion ÷ plasma concentration = 1500 \div 1.0 = 1500 dL/day = 150 L/day. Divide by 1440 min: 150\,000/1440 = 104 mL/min.

A normal GFR is about 125 mL/min, so 104 mL/min is mildly reduced but near normal. Creatinine is used because it is filtered and hardly reabsorbed, so its clearance approximates the GFR.

Step 2 — selective reabsorption

Reabsorption is selective: the tubule takes back what the body needs and leaves the waste. About 99 % of the water and 99.5 % of the sodium are recovered, along with all the glucose and amino acids.

Substance Main site Mechanism Reabsorbed
Glucose PCT secondary active transport with Na⁺ (SGLT), then facilitated diffusion out 100 % below the threshold
Amino acids PCT active transport with Na⁺ 100 %
Na⁺ PCT (65 %), ascending limb (25 %), DCT/CD (aldosterone) Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase on the basolateral side drives it 99.5 %
Water PCT (65–70 %), descending limb, collecting duct (ADH) osmosis 99 %
HCO₃⁻ PCT indirectly, as H⁺ is secreted about 90 %
Urea PCT and collecting duct diffusion (some facilitated) 40–50 %
Creatinine — not reabsorbed; some secreted 0 %

Glucose and the renal threshold. The carrier proteins can move only so much glucose per minute; their limit is the transport maximum (Tm), about 375 mg min⁻¹. As long as the filtered load stays below it, all glucose is recovered.

The plasma level at which the load reaches the Tm is the renal threshold, about 180 mg/dL. Above that, the carriers saturate and glucose appears in the urine — glycosuria.

Filtered load of glucose

Problem. Plasma glucose is 300 mg/dL and GFR is 125 mL min⁻¹. What mass of glucose is filtered each minute, and does any appear in the urine if the Tm is 375 mg min⁻¹?

Solution. 300 mg/dL = 3 mg/mL. Load = 3 \times 125 = 375 mg min⁻¹. This is exactly the Tm, so the carriers are just saturated and glucose begins to spill. At 400 mg/dL the load would be 4 \times 125 = 500 mg min⁻¹, and about 500 - 375 = 125 mg min⁻¹ would be lost.

Water and the counter-current multiplier. Water is not pumped; it follows solute by osmosis.

The loop of Henle makes that possible by creating a gradient of osmolarity in the medulla, from 300 mOsm L⁻¹ at the corticomedullary junction to 1200 mOsm L⁻¹ (up to 1400) at the papilla. The mechanism has four steps:

  1. The filtrate entering the descending limb is isotonic (300).
  2. The descending limb is permeable to water but not to solute. As it runs down into the salty medulla, water leaves by osmosis and the filtrate becomes steadily more concentrated, reaching about 1200 at the tip.
  3. The ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively pumps Na⁺ and Cl⁻ into the interstitium. Solute leaves, water cannot, so the filtrate becomes dilute — about 100 at the top.
  4. The NaCl left behind in the medulla keeps the interstitium hypertonic, and the vasa recta carry away the water without washing the salt out. Because the two limbs carry fluid in opposite directions and have opposite permeabilities, the gradient is multiplied along the length of the loop.

Level Interstitial osmolarity Filtrate in the loop
Cortex / PCT 300 300 (isotonic)
Outer medulla 400–600 descending 400–600
Inner medulla 900 descending 900
Papilla (tip) 1200 1200 at the bend
Top of ascending limb 300 100 (dilute)

The length of the loop sets the steepness of the gradient. Desert mammals such as the kangaroo rat have very long loops and make urine of 5000 mOsm L⁻¹; birds have short loops and concentrate weakly; fish have no loop at all.

The same logic explains why a long loop means a dry habitat.

The DCT and collecting duct. The DCT receives hypotonic fluid (about 100 mOsm L⁻¹). Here Na⁺ is reabsorbed under aldosterone and Ca²⁺ under parathyroid hormone.

The collecting duct is where the final decision is made: if ADH is present, its cells insert aquaporin-2 channels and water leaves into the hypertonic medulla, so the urine becomes concentrated; if ADH is absent, the duct stays almost impermeable and a large volume of dilute urine is passed.

The two limbs are not interchangeable

The descending limb is permeable to water and not to solute; the ascending limb is permeable to neither water nor (freely) solute, but pumps salt.

Any option that says "the ascending limb reabsorbs water" or "the descending limb pumps sodium" is wrong. If both limbs behaved alike, the gradient would vanish and no mammal could concentrate urine.

Step 3 — tubular secretion

Secretion moves substances from the blood of the peritubular capillaries into the tubule, the opposite direction to reabsorption. It is the tubule's way of getting rid of things that filtration alone cannot handle.

Substance Where secreted Why it matters
H⁺ PCT and intercalated cells of the collecting duct regulates blood pH; can acidify urine to pH 4.5
K⁺ principal cells of the DCT and collecting duct the main route for potassium loss; increased by aldosterone
NH₃ PCT combines with H⁺ to form NH₄⁺, trapping acid in the urine
Creatinine PCT a waste that is also filtered
Drugs PCT penicillin, aspirin, morphine, diuretics — many are protein-bound and never filtered
Organic acids and bases PCT e.g. para-aminohippuric acid (PAH), used to measure renal blood flow

Secretion matters for two reasons. First, some wastes (K⁺, H⁺) are almost entirely removed this way. Second, drugs bound to plasma proteins are too large to filter, so secretion is their only exit.

Hormonal regulation

Three hormones set the final volume and concentration of urine.

ADH (vasopressin). Made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, carried down axons and stored in the posterior pituitary, from which it is released.

Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in plasma osmolarity (as little as 2 %), and ADH is released.

It binds V₂ receptors on the collecting duct and inserts aquaporin-2 water channels, so water is reabsorbed and the urine becomes small and concentrated. A fall in osmolarity switches ADH off and a large dilute urine is produced.

Diabetes insipidus. A deficiency of ADH (or a failure of the kidney to respond to it) gives polyuria — up to 15–20 L a day of pale urine with a specific gravity of 1.001–1.005 — and intense polydipsia.

The urine is dilute because the water is not reabsorbed, not because glucose is pulling water into the tubule.

Aldosterone. A steroid from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. It increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion in the DCT and collecting duct; water follows the sodium.

The result is a small volume of urine with little sodium and more potassium, and a rise in blood pressure.

The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS). When blood pressure, blood volume or Na⁺ falls (or K⁺ rises), the juxtaglomerular cells release renin.

Renin converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mostly in the lungs, converts it to angiotensin II.

Angiotensin II is a strong vasoconstrictor and also stimulates aldosterone release, ADH release and thirst. The net effect is to retain sodium and water and raise blood pressure.

ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide). Stretch of the atria — as when blood volume rises — releases this 28-amino-acid peptide from atrial muscle cells.

ANP inhibits Na⁺ reabsorption in the collecting duct, inhibits renin and aldosterone, dilates the afferent arteriole and constricts the efferent one, so GFR rises.

The result is a large volume of sodium-rich, dilute urine and a fall in blood pressure. It is the physiological opponent of the RAAS.

Hormone Source Main action Urine volume Urine concentration
ADH hypothalamus → posterior pituitary ↑ water permeability of DCT/CD (aquaporin-2) ↓ ↑ (up to 1200 mOsm L⁻¹)
Aldosterone adrenal cortex, zona glomerulosa ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption, ↑ K⁺ secretion ↓ ↑ (water follows Na⁺)
ANP atrial muscle ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption, ↓ renin, ↑ GFR ↑ ↓ (dilute)
PTH parathyroid ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption, ↓ phosphate reabsorption little change —
The three hormones in one line

ADH saves water, aldosterone saves salt (and wastes potassium), ANP throws both away. For each, ask two questions: does urine volume go up or down? and does the urine get more or less concentrated?

Composition of urine

Property Normal value
Volume 1–2 L per day (1.5 L average)
Colour pale yellow (urochrome)
pH 4.6–8.0, average about 6
Specific gravity 1.003–1.035 (average 1.020)
Osmolarity 300–1200 mOsm L⁻¹
Water about 95 %
Urea 25–35 g per day — the most abundant solute
Uric acid 0.5–1 g per day
Creatinine 1–1.5 g per day
Others Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, sulphate, phosphate, ammonia, urobilinogen, hormones, vitamins

Abnormal constituents are the quickest route to a diagnosis, and the paper likes them as one-line matches.

Constituent What it signals
Glucose diabetes mellitus; also renal glycosuria (low threshold) and pregnancy
Protein (albumin) glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, pre-eclampsia; transient after heavy exercise or fever
Ketones starvation, uncontrolled type 1 diabetes (ketoacidosis), persistent vomiting
Blood / red cells glomerulonephritis, stones, trauma, tumour, urinary infection
Casts (hyaline, granular, red-cell) renal tubular damage; red-cell casts point to glomerulonephritis
Pus cells and nitrite urinary tract infection (cystitis, pyelonephritis)
Bilirubin obstructive jaundice, hepatitis
Crystals oxalate or urate stones, gout
hCG pregnancy (basis of the pregnancy test)
Glucose in urine is not always diabetes

Glycosuria means glucose has exceeded the renal threshold.

It happens in diabetes mellitus because the plasma level is high, but also in renal glycosuria, where the carriers themselves are faulty and the threshold is low even though blood glucose is normal.

The stem usually gives the blood glucose to separate the two.

8.3 Renal disorders

Nephritis

Nephritis is inflammation of the kidney.

The commonest form is glomerulonephritis, an immune-complex (type III) reaction: antibodies made against a β-haemolytic streptococcus (after a throat or skin infection) cross-react with the glomerular basement membrane, or antigen–antibody complexes lodge there.

It usually appears 1–3 weeks after the infection.

Features: haematuria (smoky or cola-coloured urine), proteinuria, oedema (especially around the eyes in the morning), hypertension and oliguria (less urine). Most children recover; some progress to chronic renal failure.

Nephrotic syndrome is a related picture with heavy protein loss, low blood albumin and generalised oedema.

Kidney stones (renal calculi)

Stones form when salts in concentrated urine crystallise. About 75–80 % are calcium oxalate; others are uric acid, cystine and struvite (the last is associated with infection).

Risk factors are a low fluid intake, a hot climate, hypercalcaemia, a diet high in oxalate (spinach, rhubarb, nuts, tea), gout and repeated urinary infection.

A stone causes renal colic — severe pain from the loin to the groin as it moves down the ureter — with haematuria and sometimes obstruction and infection.

Small stones pass with fluids and analgesia; larger ones are broken by extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) or removed through a ureteroscope.

Renal failure

Renal failure is a fall in GFR severe enough to retain waste.

Acute renal failure Chronic renal failure
Onset hours to days months to years
Common causes shock, severe dehydration, blood loss, nephrotoxic drugs, obstruction diabetes mellitus and hypertension (the two commonest), glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney
Reversible? often, if the cause is corrected no; progressive
Features oliguria or anuria, rising urea and creatinine, high K⁺ uraemia, anaemia (less erythropoietin), acidosis, oedema, bone disease

When the kidneys fail, urea and creatinine rise (uraemia), K⁺ rises (hyperkalaemia, dangerous for the heart), H⁺ accumulates (acidosis) and erythropoietin falls (anaemia). Treatment is by dialysis or transplantation.

Dialysis

Dialysis filters the blood through a semipermeable membrane against a dialysate whose concentration is set so that wastes diffuse out while useful substances stay.

Haemodialysis Peritoneal dialysis
Membrane cellulose or synthetic membrane in a dialyser the peritoneum
Blood flow pumped from an arteriovenous fistula the patient's own capillaries
Schedule 3–4 hours, 2–3 times a week, in hospital 4–6 hour dwells, about 4 exchanges a day, at home
Efficiency high lower
Main risk clotting (heparin used), hypotension, infection of the access peritonitis

In haemodialysis the blood and the dialysate flow in opposite directions (counter-current), which keeps a concentration gradient along the whole membrane so that diffusion does not stop halfway.

Kidney transplantation

A healthy kidney from a living related donor or a cadaver is placed in the iliac fossa and joined to the iliac vessels and the bladder. The donor and recipient are matched for ABO and HLA antigens.

The recipient takes immunosuppressant drugs (ciclosporin, tacrolimus, steroids) for life to prevent rejection.

A working transplant gives a better quality of life and longer survival than dialysis, but the supply of organs is far short of the need.

The three numbers to hold

125 mL min⁻¹ (GFR) → 180 L day⁻¹ (filtrate) → 1.5 L day⁻¹ (urine): 99 % reabsorbed. 180 mg/dL is the renal threshold for glucose, 1200 mOsm L⁻¹ the maximum urine concentration. These three facts answer a large share of the numerical questions.

Chapter summary

  • The excretory organs are the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra; the skin, lungs and liver are accessory routes, and the liver makes urea while the kidney excretes it.
  • Each kidney has about one million nephrons, in a cortex (corpuscles, convoluted tubules) and a medulla (pyramids, loops, collecting ducts) that drains through the pelvis into the ureter.
  • Ultrafiltration at the glomerulus passes water and small solutes but holds back cells and protein by pore size and negative charge; net pressure ≈ 10 mmHg, GFR ≈ 125 mL min⁻¹ (180 L day⁻¹).
  • Reabsorption recovers about 99 % of the filtrate: glucose and amino acids by active transport in the PCT (threshold 180 mg/dL, Tm 375 mg min⁻¹), water by osmosis.
  • The counter-current multiplier works because the descending limb is permeable to water and the ascending limb is not but pumps salt; the medulla is graded 300 → 1200 mOsm L⁻¹, and the vasa recta preserve the gradient.
  • Secretion adds H⁺, K⁺, NH₃, creatinine and drugs to the tubule and is the main route for acid removal.
  • ADH (made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary) concentrates urine; aldosterone retains Na⁺ and loses K⁺; ANP does the opposite. Diabetes insipidus = ADH problem = large dilute urine; diabetes mellitus = insulin problem = large glucose-containing urine.
  • Abnormal constituents: glucose (diabetes), protein (nephritis), ketones (starvation, ketoacidosis), blood (nephritis, stones), casts (tubular damage).
  • Disorders: nephritis, calcium oxalate stones, acute and chronic failure; haemodialysis uses a dialyser, peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneum, and transplantation needs HLA matching and lifelong immunosuppression.

Model answer D1: Excretory organs and the nephron (10 marks)

Introduction. Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes such as urea, uric acid, creatinine and carbon dioxide. Humans are ureotelic, as the main waste is urea made in the liver.

Excretory organs.

  1. Kidneys: a pair of bean-shaped organs behind the abdominal cavity, each about 10 cm long, that make urine and keep water, salt and pH balanced.
  2. Ureters: muscular tubes that carry urine to the bladder by peristalsis.
  3. Urinary bladder: stores urine (about 300–500 mL) with transitional epithelium.
  4. Urethra: carries urine out; about 4 cm in women and 20 cm in men.
  5. Other organs: skin (sweat: water, salts, a little urea), lungs (CO₂, water vapour) and liver (bile pigments).

Structure of the kidney. A tough capsule covers the kidney. The outer cortex and inner medulla (with 8–18 pyramids) lead into the renal pelvis. Each kidney has about one million nephrons.

Structure of a nephron.

Part Structure Function
Malpighian body Bowman's capsule + glomerulus (a tuft of capillaries) Ultrafiltration of blood
PCT (proximal convoluted tubule) Cuboidal cells with brush border Reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, salts, water
Loop of Henle Descending and ascending limbs in the medulla Concentrates the urine
DCT (distal convoluted tubule) Cuboidal cells Selective reabsorption and secretion of K⁺, H⁺
Collecting duct Receives urine from many nephrons Final water reabsorption; leads to pelvis

Blood enters the glomerulus by the afferent arteriole (wider) and leaves through the efferent arteriole (narrower), so a high pressure builds up.

Cortical nephrons have short loops and juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops and are important in concentrating urine. The vasa recta are capillaries along the loop.

Conclusion. The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney, with each part adapted to filter, reabsorb or secrete.

Model answer D2: Urine formation, regulation and disorders (10 marks)

Introduction. Urine is formed in three steps in the nephron: ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption and tubular secretion.

  1. Ultrafiltration (glomerulus): the high pressure (about 60 mm Hg) forces water, glucose, salts, amino acids and urea through three layers (capillary endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes) into Bowman's capsule. Proteins and blood cells stay behind. The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 125 mL/min, or 125 × 60 × 24 = 180 litres a day.
  2. Selective reabsorption: nearly all glucose and amino acids, and about 65% of water and Na⁺, return to the blood in the PCT by active transport and diffusion.
  3. Tubular secretion: H⁺, K⁺, ammonia and drugs pass from blood to tubule, mainly in the DCT, which controls blood pH.
  4. Concentration of urine: the loop of Henle and vasa recta work as a counter-current system, producing a salty medulla (up to 1200 mOsm/L). Water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis.

Only about 1.5 L of urine is made per day, so 180 − 1.5 = 178.5 L is reabsorbed, i.e. 99.2%. Normal urine is pale yellow, acidic (pH about 6), with 95% water and 2.5% urea.

Regulation.

Hormone Gland Action
ADH (vasopressin) Posterior pituitary Makes the collecting duct permeable to water; urine becomes concentrated
Aldosterone Adrenal cortex Increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion
Renin–angiotensin Juxtaglomerular cells Raises blood pressure; releases aldosterone
ANF Atria of heart Opposes renin; lowers BP and increases urine

Renal disorders.

  1. Kidney stones (renal calculi): crystals of calcium oxalate or phosphate; severe pain.
  2. Glomerulonephritis: inflammation of glomeruli, often after a throat infection.
  3. Uraemia: build-up of urea in the blood when the kidneys fail.
  4. Diabetes insipidus: lack of ADH, giving large volumes of dilute urine.
  5. Treatment: haemodialysis (a dialysing machine cleans the blood through a membrane) or a kidney transplant, available in Nepal at several hospitals.

Conclusion. The kidney filters 180 L of fluid daily and returns nearly all of it, keeping the body's internal environment steady.
